regions.name: Middle East
overview: The Saudi–Houthi war has become the region's deadliest front. A Houthi missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 10 October, killing 12–13 people and wounding 309, and the coalition says strikes on the airport from 7 to 11 October killed 17 and wounded 333 in total. The airport is still closed, a Saudi Aramco building in Dhahran was hit on 14 October, and a missile was intercepted near Medina on 15 October. In Yemen, government forces claim advances in Marib and Taiz under Operation Dawn of Yemen, while Houthi missiles hit the presidential palace in Aden on 15 October. Riyadh says the Houthis refused talks in Oman.

Iran stepped up its campaign against shipping at Hormuz to the highest tempo of the war, with at least 10 ships struck from 11 October and four UKMTO reports on that day alone. The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after being hit on 13 October; Iran says it struck a mine, while CENTCOM says it was an IRGC projectile. Trump has said there will be no US strikes on Iran before the 3 November midterms but is keeping the naval blockade. Netanyahu is reportedly considering renewed strikes on Iran, and Pezeshkian calls the blockade the most intense since 1979.

Israel kept its periphery under steady fire in the run-up to the 27 October election. In Gaza the toll since the ceasefire reached 1,493 killed by 12 October, and the area under Israeli control has grown to about 63% of the Strip. Israel kept up daily shelling and lethal fire in south Lebanon and made near-daily incursions into Quneitra and western Daraa. Settler attacks during the West Bank olive harvest averaged 12–19 a day.

Non-state armed actors are filling security gaps. Lebanon seized about 500 kg of TNT and C-4 that Hezbollah publicly claimed on 15 October, defying the state's monopoly on weapons. In Iraq, ISIS killed an army brigadier general and two soldiers near Kirkuk on 14 October, two weeks after the US exit, while Kataib Hezbollah openly praised Houthi strikes on Riyadh and issued demands to Saudi Arabia.

countries.name: Gaza
incidents: 10 Oct — Western Gaza City: An Israeli drone strike near Panda Mall killed 4 Palestinians, whom Israel called Hamas Nukhba members; Israeli fire on a tent separately killed an 8-year-old girl.
11 Oct — Khan Younis: An Israeli drone strike on a phone-charging point west of the city killed 4 people, according to Wafa.
12 Oct — Al-Mawasi (south Gaza): An Israeli drone strike near a mosque killed 2 young men; the Health Ministry put the toll since the ceasefire at 1,493 killed and 5,299 wounded.
14 Oct — Gaza City: An Israeli air strike on an apartment block killed a woman and wounded 2; the IDF separately said it had killed a Hamas commander who held hostages during the war.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. One year into the ceasefire, deadly Israeli strikes now come almost daily: 33 more people were killed in a single week. Israel has pushed the Yellow Line further into residential parts of Gaza City and now controls about 63% of the Strip. Phase two (Israeli withdrawal and Hamas disarmament) is stalled, aid stays far below the agreed 600 trucks a day, and reconstruction has not begun. Over the next 90 days, expect continued targeted strikes on alleged Hamas and Islamic Jihad operatives in residential areas, with civilian deaths, and further creeping expansion of the Israeli-held zone. Little movement is likely until a new Israeli government is formed after the 27 October election, and the risk of a wider resumption of operations rises if attacks on IDF troops along the Yellow Line increase. Humanitarian conditions will worsen as winter sets in.

countries.name: Lebanon
incidents: 10 Oct — Bint Jbeil and Nabatieh districts: Israeli artillery shelled Mansouri, Wadi Zibqine, Aita al-Jabal, Braasheet, Haddatha, Mayfadoun and Kfar Tibnit overnight; an Israeli drone struck Kfar Tibnit the next night.

11 Oct — Bint Jbeil district (Yater, Froun): A man inspecting his olive grove was killed by Israeli tank fire on the outskirts of Yater, and a second man died in Froun when leftover Israeli ordnance exploded; the Lebanese army called it a 'flagrant breach' of existing agreements.

~10 and 12 Oct — Bekaa/Hermel: The Lebanese army seized a vehicle carrying about 500 kg of TNT and C-4 headed for Beirut, arresting two Hezbollah members, and seized another 200 kg of explosives smuggled from Syria near Hermel; PM Salam warned that C-4 is 'used in political assassinations'.

15 Oct — Beirut: Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah said the seized explosives belonged to Hezbollah and were meant 'to confront the Israeli occupation', openly defying the government's ban on weapons outside the state.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israeli artillery, tank and drone fire on the south continues every day from the strip Israel occupies, with civilian deaths during the olive harvest, and more than 4,300 people have been killed since March. Hezbollah's public claim to the seized explosives is a direct challenge to the government's disarmament push and raises the risk of confrontation between the state and the group. Over the next 90 days, expect continued Israeli strikes and possible deeper raids. Watch for internal friction if the army keeps up its seizures, and for continued Hezbollah rearmament via Syria. The end of UNIFIL's mandate on 31 December, with no agreed follow-on force, will widen the security gap south of the Litani. An Israeli withdrawal is unlikely before a new Israeli government is in place.

countries.name: Iran
incidents: 9 Oct — Gulf (13 nm west of the UAE's Al Jazeera): A VLCC was struck by an unknown projectile and caught fire, which was later put out.

11 Oct — Strait of Hormuz: UKMTO reported four attacks in one day on three tankers and an inbound container ship; IRGC-affiliated media showed the VLCC Al Maqam, which it said was transiting without authorisation, and at least 10 ships were struck in and around Hormuz over the following days.

13 Oct — South of the Strait of Hormuz: The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride was hit and later sank (all 21 crew safe), and its sister ship GFS Giselle was also struck; the IRGC claimed a mine strike, CENTCOM said an IRGC projectile, and Iran also claimed a hit on an ADNOC VLCC.

14–15 Oct — Kerman/Tehran: Iran executed January protester Ali-Sina Mostafavi for 'moharebeh'; on 15 Oct a tanker caught fire in the Gulf of Oman after entering an Iranian 'prohibited zone', and Pezeshkian said Iran faces its most intense blockade since 1979.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The war with the US has not ended: the US naval blockade continues, and Iran has escalated its use of force at sea to the highest tempo of the war, sinking a container ship and striking at least 10 vessels in a week. Indirect talks through mediators continue, but Tehran is still reviewing US proposals and there is no agreed framework. Trump has ruled out US strikes before the 3 November midterms, but reports that Netanyahu is considering renewed strikes, and that the US is weighing heavy ordnance options, point to a high risk of strikes on Iranian territory after the US election. Over the next 90 days, expect continued tanker attacks and claims of Hormuz control, further executions of January protesters, and Iranian encouragement of the Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia. A deal is unlikely before mid-November at the earliest.

countries.name: Yemen
incidents: 13 Oct — Marib/Taiz: Government forces claimed strategic advances into Marib governorate under Operation Dawn of Yemen, while Houthi shelling of residential areas of besieged Taiz caused dozens of civilian casualties; food shortages were reported in the city.

14 Oct — Nationwide: The government claimed 2,309 'targeting operations' and 460 Houthi vehicles destroyed, plus the recapture of Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz; the WFP warned that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted (government claims unverified).

14–15 Oct — West of Taiz (Mount Han): Government forces repelled a major Houthi attempt to seize strategic positions; coalition jets struck Houthi positions in Sanaa and around al-Misrakh and at-Turbah.

15 Oct — Aden: Houthi ballistic missiles hit the al-Maashiq presidential palace complex, killing 2–4 members of PM al-Zandani's security detail (AFP sources say 4 killed and 10 wounded); Marib city was also targeted.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Full-scale war continues on several fronts: the Red Sea coast, Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf. Saudi air power supports government ground advances, while the Houthis strike Aden, Marib and Saudi cities with ballistic missiles. The ICRC reports front-line hospitals receiving more than 700 weapon-wounded patients a week. Government territorial claims remain largely unverified and the Houthis deny losing ground. Over the next 90 days, expect grinding ground battles around Taiz and Marib rather than a breakthrough toward Sanaa, continued Houthi missile fire on Aden and the government leadership, and a severe humanitarian crisis as the Taiz siege, food stock depletion and cholera worsen. Houthi refusal of Oman-hosted talks makes a ceasefire unlikely in the short term. Possible US involvement, which Trump has floated, would be a major escalator.

countries.name: Israel
incidents: 8 Oct — South Lebanon: IDF Capt. Eliav Haim Tzapalamus (21) was killed when a military vehicle overturned during operations, the IDF said, describing it as an operational accident.

9–11 Oct — West Bank: The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 19, 12 and 18 settler attacks on consecutive days; in al-Mughayyir, soldiers fired live rounds and tear gas into houses during a settler incursion.
Week of 9–13 Oct — West Bank (Deir Abu Mash'al): Settlers attacked a solidarity olive harvest in Area B, wounding 8, including a photojournalist shot in the thigh.

~14 Oct — Jerusalem: Netanyahu was reported to be seriously considering resuming strikes on Iran, while Trump had ruled out US strikes before the 3 November midterms; the IDF chief of staff reportedly warned that a strike could delay the 27 October election.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. No missile, rocket or drone attacks on Israeli territory were found this week; Israel's war fronts are outside its borders, in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. Inside the country and the West Bank, the threat is recurring violence: daily settler attacks during the olive harvest, IDF raids and ongoing militant activity. Over the next 90 days, the main escalation risk is a renewed Israeli strike on Iran after the election or after the US midterms, which would very likely bring Iranian and possibly Houthi missile fire on Israel and put the country back at CRITICAL. Hezbollah's open claim to stockpiled explosives and the build-up of Houthi long-range capability are also risks. Expect elevated West Bank violence around the 27 October election and through the end of the harvest.

countries.name: Iraq
incidents: 12 Oct — Baghdad: Kataib Hezbollah reportedly praised the Houthi strike on Riyadh and issued three demands to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman ahead of PM al-Zaidi's planned Saudi visit, while maintaining that it is not bound by any disarmament timetable.

13–14 Oct — South of Kirkuk: Iraqi warplanes struck an ISIS hideout about 80 km south of Kirkuk; the next day a roadside bomb hit the army patrol searching the site, killing Brig. Gen. Ahat Yasser Khudair Hussein and a warrant officer, and a third soldier later died of his wounds.
15 Oct — Washington/Baghdad: The US Treasury sanctioned Iran-linked financial networks, including an Iraqi bank.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. ISIS is exploiting the post-US security gap in the Kirkuk–Hawija belt, with deadly attacks on 5 and 14 October, the latter killing a brigadier general. Iraq still does not fit CRITICAL, however: there is no sustained armed conflict on its territory, and no militia rocket or drone attacks on Iraqi or Kurdish targets were found. Over the next 90 days, the main risks are further ISIS IED and ambush attacks in Kirkuk, Salahuddin, Nineveh and Anbar, and hardline militias (Kataib Hezbollah, Nujaba) resuming drone attacks on Saudi Arabia in support of the Houthis, which happened in July and drew joint US-Saudi strikes on PMF bases. US secondary sanctions on Iraqi banks will also add economic pressure. A return to CRITICAL is plausible if Iraqi territory again becomes a launch pad or target in the US–Iran or Saudi–Houthi wars.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
incidents: 10 Oct — Riyadh: A Houthi missile struck King Khalid International Airport, killing 12–13 people (Saudis, Bangladeshis, and nationals of the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine, Sudan and India) and wounding 309; the airport has since stayed closed.

11 Oct — Riyadh: A further Houthi strike on King Khalid Airport killed a Pakistani resident and wounded 11; the coalition said attacks on the airport killed 17 and wounded 333 between 7 and 11 October, and that it has been targeted 20 times since 1 October.
14 Oct — Dhahran: The Houthis claimed attacks on Aramco and a Riyadh refinery; an Energy Ministry official confirmed a building in Dhahran was hit, causing a 'limited fire' with no casualties.

15 Oct — Medina/Khamis Mushait: The coalition said it intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region (denied by the Houthis), a missile aimed at Riyadh and a drone over Khamis Mushait; Riyadh said the Houthis had refused to meet in Oman and the EU–GCC summit planned for 24 October was postponed.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained and intensifying. The 10 October Riyadh airport strike was the deadliest Houthi attack on Saudi soil in this war. Combined with the strike on Aramco in Dhahran and the threat to Medina, the Houthi campaign now reaches the capital, the Eastern Province energy hub and the holy cities. Over the next 90 days, expect continued ballistic missile and drone salvos on Riyadh, Abha, Jizan, Najran, Khamis Mushait and energy sites, a prolonged closure or disruption of the Riyadh airport, airline suspensions, and the cancellation of major events. Riyadh will seek deeper US involvement, which Trump has said is possible, and support from allies under defence agreements (Turkey and Pakistan have reportedly agreed to send forces). Iraqi militias could also resume drone attacks. A ceasefire is unlikely while the Houthis refuse talks and the ground offensive continues.

countries.name: Syria
incidents: 11–12 Oct — Quneitra/western Daraa: Israeli forces detained three young men from Abu Muthara during an incursion via the Abu al-Ghaithar gate, releasing them the next day; on 12 Oct a two-vehicle force fired heavy weapons near Wadi al-Raqad (Syrian state media).

14 Oct — Southern Quneitra/Daraa: An eight-vehicle Israeli force pushed in west of al-Hanout farm, expelled shepherds and fired on a civilian water tanker; a separate patrol raided a house in Wadi al-Raqad, briefly detained young men and seized a motorcycle (SANA).

15 Oct — Western Daraa (Wadi al-Raqad): A five-vehicle Israeli force advanced into the area and set fire to a warehouse and a house, according to SANA; Syrian state media also reports a fortified Israeli 'Sufa 53' line about 80% complete along a roughly 70 km strip from Mount Hermon to the Yarmouk.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israeli forces hold and keep fortifying a de facto security zone in Quneitra and western Daraa, with near-daily incursions, detentions, arson and fire on civilians. Suwayda remains outside effective state control, and Damascus accuses Israel of trying to destabilise it. No deadly clashes were confirmed this week, but the foreign military presence and the loss of state control over parts of the south have not decreased. Over the next 90 days, expect continued Israeli raids and construction of fortifications, a risk of Israeli strikes if government forces deploy south, a renewed Druze–government flare-up in Suwayda, and continued Hezbollah weapons smuggling across the Lebanese border. The US-supervised Syria–Israel communication mechanism is unlikely to produce a security deal before a new Israeli government is formed.

countries.name: Egypt
incidents: 10 Oct — Riyadh (Saudi Arabia): Egyptian flight attendant Azza Ramzi Mohamed Hassan (28) was among those killed in the Houthi strike on King Khalid International Airport; the Egyptian embassy is arranging repatriation.

Early Oct — Suez Canal: The Suez Canal Authority said the canal is safe and traffic regular, reporting August revenue of $567.1 million, up 56.7% year on year, despite continued tension around Bab al-Mandeb.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No armed violence, terrorist attack or military incident on Egyptian territory was found this week. Egypt's exposure is through its citizens in the Gulf, its role as a Gaza mediator and the Red Sea shipping route. Over the next 90 days, the main risks are escalation around Bab al-Mandeb that cuts Suez revenue (the Houthis are already targeting Saudi-linked shipping), any Egyptian naval role in the Red Sea that makes Egypt a Houthi target, and spillover along the Rafah border if Gaza escalates. Domestic security is likely to stay tight. A return to HIGH would require direct attacks on Egyptian assets or a significant terrorist incident in Sinai.

countries.name: Jordan
incidents: 14 Oct — Northern and western borders: Jordan has stepped up border patrols and upgraded surveillance in response to a rise in drug smuggling by balloon and quadcopter from Israel, according to a Jordan Times report citing The Telegraph; the army regularly downs smuggling drones coming from Syria.

15–16 Oct — Jordan: CENTCOM dismissed as false Iranian claims that hundreds of US service members had been killed in Jordan, stating that 3 US personnel were killed in the July attacks; no new strike on Jordanian territory was independently confirmed.
9–16 Oct — Jordanian airspace: No confirmed Iranian missile or drone strike on Jordan was reported, extending the lull since the 9 September barrage on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base to about five weeks.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. No confirmed attack on Jordanian territory has been reported for about five weeks, but Jordan hosts a growing US force that redeployed from Iraq, and the IRGC is making propaganda claims about mass US casualties there, which shows the bases remain in Iran's sights. Trump's pledge not to strike Iran before the 3 November midterms lowers the near-term risk, but any post-election US or Israeli strike on Iran would very likely trigger renewed Iranian barrages on US bases in Jordan, putting it back at CRITICAL. Over the next 90 days, expect sustained high air-defence alert and continued drone and balloon smuggling of drugs and weapons across the Syrian and Israeli borders, with Jordanian countermeasures.

countries.name: Libya
incidents: 26 Sep — Sharara–Zawiya pipeline: Several outlets reported the NOC reopened the pipeline after a five-day forced closure by armed guards that cost about $95 million; the Security Council Report's October forecast still lists the closure as a key development, so the current status is unclear.

3 Oct (reported) — Tripoli: GNU sources told the Guardian that suspects detained over drone attacks on fuel and power infrastructure in western Libya were working for Saddam Haftar, throwing the US-backed east–west unity effort into doubt.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No new armed clashes or attacks were found for 9–16 October; the latest developments are the coercive closure of the Sharara pipeline and the alleged link between Saddam Haftar and drone sabotage in the west. ACLED counts more than 30 armed clashes in Zawiya in 2026, so the underlying instability persists and Libya sits at the upper end of MODERATE. Over the next 90 days, watch the renewal of UNSMIL's mandate (which expires on 31 October), further shutdowns of oil infrastructure by armed groups, drone attacks on western energy sites, and a possible government offensive against Mohamed Bahroun's forces in Zawiya. Any of these would justify HIGH. A return to full-scale east–west war is unlikely.

countries.name: Tunisia
incidents: 14 Oct — Tunis: A court freed activists Aya Sadraoui and Ghaith Hamrouni; 11 named participants in the September Sumud solidarity march have left custody since 6 Oct, at least six of them with suspended sentences of 6–12 months.

15 Oct — Tunis: Protesters marched again in solidarity with the four jailed Global Sumud Flotilla organisers on hunger strike; no arrests were reported. Separately, the journalists' union says about 20 journalists face criminal charges and four are imprisoned.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Tunisia still fits MODERATE: protests and judicial repression with no violence and no organised armed threat. The release of the September detainees with suspended sentences suggests some short-term de-escalation, but the core grievance, the four jailed flotilla organisers on a prolonged hunger strike, remains. Over the next 90 days, a death or medical collapse among the hunger strikers is the most likely trigger for larger unrest. Expect continued prosecutions of journalists and opposition figures, economic frustration, and secondary risk from instability and fuel smuggling along the western Libyan border.

regions.name: Ukraine/Russia
overview: US policy shifted sharply this week, and not in Kyiv's favour. On 9 October Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin (OFAC General License 135, up to 4.8 million tonnes). On 10 October he called for Zelensky to be replaced and blamed Ukrainian refinery strikes for high fuel prices. On 11 October he declared a unilateral 'energy ceasefire' that Moscow never confirmed. Kyiv also reported that its military Starlink/Starshield access had been throttled and that the US had threatened to withhold intelligence. Putin told Trump that an early resumption of peace talks was unlikely.

The energy truce collapsed within days. Ukraine paused refinery strikes for about three days while Russia kept hitting the grid, including drone strikes on Kyiv on 13–14 October. On the night of 15 October Russia launched more than 850 drones at 15 regions, killing at least 17 people. That day Zelensky lifted the pause, and Ukraine struck the Ryazan refinery (15 Oct) and the Saratov refinery (16 Oct). Zelensky said a renewed pause would require Patriot deliveries, and Ukraine's interceptor stocks are reported to be critically low again.

Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities stayed mass-casualty in scale: a glide-bomb strike on Zaporizhzhia on 10 October killed about 20, and a missile strike on a Kharkiv grocery store on 11 October killed 3. Ukraine kept up deep strikes, including the Ukhta refinery (9 Oct), drones that briefly closed all four Moscow airports (11 Oct), a claimed Neptune strike that destroyed four Su-34s (15 Oct), and a Yandex data centre in Vladimir Oblast (16 Oct). Europe is moving apart from Washington, with UK Storm Shadow resupply reported and EU asset talks held without the US.

On the periphery, pressure continues without open hostilities. Drones entered Moldovan airspace on 11 and 15 October; one crashed and exploded on Moldovan soil, and 56 violations have been recorded so far in 2026. CSTO drills with more than 1,500 troops ran in Belarus on 11/12–16 October. Georgia's Constitutional Court has begun hearing the party-ban case and the opposition has called a protest campaign for 25 October. Azerbaijan saw school-hijab protests, 37 detentions and reported social-media throttling. Armenia–Russia friction grew after a ruling-party MP was refused entry to Russia.

countries.name: Ukraine
incidents: 10 Oct — Zaporizhzhia: Russia dropped five glide bombs on residential buildings, killing about 20 people, including 3 children (Reuters). It was the third mass-casualty attack of the week, after Pryluky and the 8 Oct bomb strike in Kramatorsk that killed at least 33.

11 Oct — Kharkiv/western Ukraine: A Russian missile hit a grocery store on the outskirts of Kharkiv, killing 3 and injuring about 20, including 2 children. A separate strike in western Ukraine killed 3 more (Reuters).

13–14 Oct — Kyiv: Russian strikes damaged a building in the capital and drone swarms hit the country during the US-declared 'energy ceasefire'. Kyiv says Russia kept attacking the power grid throughout, while Ukraine held off refinery strikes for about three days.

15 Oct — Nationwide/Kirovohrad/Kyiv: Russia launched more than 850 drones at 15 regions, killing at least 17 and injuring 67. It was the largest-ever attack on Kirovohrad region (3 killed); parts of Kyiv lost power and water pressure. Zelensky then lifted the pause on strikes against Russian refineries.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Ukraine is under full-scale attack and mass-casualty strikes happen several times a week. Over the next 90 days, expect Russia to intensify its winter campaign against the grid with record drone salvos (850+ in one night), glide bombs on frontline cities and ballistic strikes on Kyiv. The aim appears to be multi-day blackouts that push civilians out of the cities. The decisive variable has shifted from Moscow to Washington. The diesel deal, Trump's call for Zelensky's replacement, the throttling of Starlink/Starshield and threats to cut intelligence and PURL deliveries all reduce Kyiv's ability to defend itself just as Patriot interceptor stocks run critically low. Expect Kyiv to lean harder on Europe (Storm Shadow resupply, frozen-asset financing, the EU summit) and to keep its refinery campaign as its main leverage. It will offer a renewed energy pause only in return for Patriots or Russian reciprocity. A durable energy truce before winter is unlikely. Watch for whether the Witkoff/Kushner visit to Moscow happens, for further US restrictions on intelligence or Starlink, and for damage to the external power supply of nuclear plants.

countries.name: Russia
incidents: 9 Oct — Ukhta (Komi Republic): A Ukrainian drone strike hit Lukoil's Ukhta refinery, which Zelensky said had been destroyed. It followed strikes on the Salavat (Bashkortostan) and Omsk refineries on 8 Oct.

11 Oct — Moscow/Bryansk/Belgorod: Ukrainian drones briefly closed all four Moscow airports (Sobyanin claimed 23 drones downed, at least 25 flights diverted). Drone strikes killed one civilian in Bryansk region (Sluchok) and one on the Posokhovo–Kazinka road in Belgorod region, where three others were wounded.

15 Oct — Ryazan/unspecified airbase: After Zelensky ended the energy pause, Ukrainian drones set the Ryazan refinery on fire. Kyiv also claimed Neptune missiles destroyed four Su-34 bombers and damaged two more (unverified).

16 Oct — Saratov/Vladimir Oblast: Ukraine's Special Operations Forces confirmed an overnight drone strike on the Saratov refinery. Drones also reportedly hit a Yandex data centre and warehouses in Vladimir Oblast.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Russia is waging an active war, and its territory, from the border oblasts to the Moscow region and refineries 2,500 km deep, is under near-daily attack with fatalities. Over the next 90 days, expect the Kremlin to bank its diplomatic gains with Washington: the diesel deal and General License 135, the partial lifting of its diesel export ban, and the US–Kyiv rift. It is likely to stall formal talks ('contacts are ongoing') while keeping up mass drone and missile strikes on the Ukrainian grid. Moscow will use any further Ukrainian refinery strikes to drive a wedge between Kyiv and Trump. With the pause over, Ukraine's deep-strike campaign is likely to resume at scale, possibly with renewed UK Storm Shadow supply. That means continued refinery outages, regional fuel strain, airport closures and civilian casualties in Belgorod, Bryansk and Kursk regions. A Witkoff/Kushner visit to Moscow is possible within two weeks. Regime stability risk remains low.

countries.name: Belarus
incidents: 11/12–16 Oct — Vitebsk region (Losvido range): The CSTO's Indestructible Brotherhood-2026 peacekeeping exercise and the Barrier-2026 biological-threat drill ran with more than 1,500 troops from Belarus, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. More than 300 pieces of equipment took part, including about 80 UAV types. The CSTO says the drills are not directed at third countries.

12 Oct — Belarus: The rights monitor iSANS put the cumulative number of recognised political prisoners since 2020 at 4,815, with 25 newly recognised in September. Lukashenka pardoned 13 more, continuing the transactional prisoner-release track with Washington.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Re-tested against the definitions, Belarus has no hostilities on its own territory. Its profile remains military activity that creates tension (CSTO drills, a Russian Oreshnik deployment, readiness checks near the Suwałki corridor) combined with low-cost hybrid pressure on Lithuania and Poland. No new balloon or airspace incident from Belarus was found this week. Over the next 90 days, expect Minsk to use the drills for signalling, to keep using prisoner releases to win US sanctions relief (potash, Lakokraska, Bellesbumprom), and possibly to resume smuggling-balloon flights over the winter, which could again close Vilnius airport or border crossings. There is no indication that Belarusian forces will enter the war. A rise to HIGH would require direct military coercion against NATO neighbours or a serious border incident.

countries.name: Moldova
incidents: 11 Oct — Moldova: During a Russian attack on Ukraine, a drone crashed and exploded on Moldovan territory without being detected by air surveillance (Ukrinform, citing Moldovan authorities). No casualties were reported.

14 Oct — Chișinău: Government institutions were targeted by cyber attacks delivered by email, and the Venice Commission urged a review of the rules for withdrawing deputies' mandates and protecting the opposition.

15 Oct — Ștefan Vodă district: During the 850-drone Russian attack, a drone entered from Ukraine's Odesa region at 01:43, flew toward Purcari and left eight minutes later. Defence Minister Nosatîi called it 'definitely Russian'. Moldova has logged 56 airspace violations in 2026.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Repeated drone incursions, including another detonation on Moldovan soil and the 3 October overflight by missiles and drones, show that spillover from Russian strikes is now constant. There are still no hostilities directed at Moldova and no casualties. Over the next 90 days, expect more incursions during each Russian mass attack on Odesa and southern Ukraine, an accelerated EU-funded acquisition of air defence and drone interceptors (EUR 120 million), and continued Russian hybrid pressure. That pressure includes cyber attacks, the opposition's push against President Sandu, influence operations around the Gagauzia People's Assembly election, and a possible winter energy squeeze on Transnistria. A first fatality from debris or a deliberate strike would warrant a review toward HIGH.

countries.name: Georgia
incidents: 12–13 Oct — Tbilisi: The Constitutional Court rejected a judge's request to recuse herself from Georgian Dream's party-ban lawsuit. Judge Manana Kobakhidze then resigned from the court (Civil.ge).

13–14 Oct — Strasbourg/Tbilisi: The Venice Commission criticised Georgia's new restrictions on foreign funding, including their criminal penalties, and the 2025 amendments that extend party bans to individuals.
14 Oct — Turkey: Opposition figure Zurab Japaridze was reportedly detained in Turkey on his way to Brussels and is to be returned to Georgia (Civil.ge headline; details unconfirmed).

15 Oct — Tbilisi: The Constitutional Court began hearing the party-ban case. The nine-party Opposition Alliance announced a protest campaign starting with a rally on 25 October titled 'Georgia without Ivanishvili'.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There is no organised political violence, and protests remain low-intensity, but the party-ban case is now formally under way before a reshaped court that has just lost a dissenting judge. Over the next 90 days, expect Georgian Dream to push the case toward a ruling, possibly around the year-end holidays. Expect continued prosecutions and travel restrictions on opposition figures (as in the Japaridze case), tighter NGO and media rules despite Venice Commission criticism, and a growing rift with the EU. The 25 October opposition rally is the first test of whether mobilisation can grow again. A ruling that bans the main opposition parties, or a violent dispersal of mass protests, would justify a return to HIGH.

countries.name: Armenia
incidents: ~10–12 Oct — Syunik/Yerevan: Pashinyan called the Shaki shooting by Azerbaijani soldier Nasimi Musayev a 'criminal incident' that does not threaten the peace process. He said the soldier will be tried in Armenia and that Baku has not requested extradition. The opposition and the victim criticised the government for failing to warn residents.

Mid-Oct — Kuris (Syunik): The National Security Service called claims that three Azerbaijanis in civilian clothes had been seen in the village 'misinformation'. The village head confirmed only an unspecified night-time incident.

14 Oct — Russia: Lusine Badalyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract party, was refused entry to Russia without explanation while travelling to a CIS conference, a new sign of deteriorating Armenia–Russia relations.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no hostilities, and the border has seen no fatal fire for more than two years. The Shaki case is being handled as a criminal matter by both governments rather than as a military incident. Over the next 90 days, expect Armenia to keep moving toward the US and EU and normalising with Turkey. Moscow is likely to retaliate with entry bans, economic pressure and influence operations; Pashinyan has said relations with Russia 'can no longer be the same'. The peace track with Azerbaijan holds but the treaty is unsigned and TRIPP has slipped to 2027. The Musayev trial, rumours of Azerbaijani infiltration and domestic polarisation are the main sources of friction. Repeated armed border crossings or a deliberate shooting incident would warrant a review toward HIGH.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
incidents: From 9 Oct — Baku/Masally/Jalilabad: Schools began barring girls who wear headscarves under a 21 September uniform decree. This set off protests at schools, solidarity walkouts by boys and a student strike.

12 Oct — Baku: The Interior Ministry said 37 people were detained for 'grossly violating public order' in school confrontations. Users reported Instagram and TikTok throttling; NetBlocks confirmation is disputed.
15 Oct — Baku: Activist İlkin Huseynov, who organised tutoring for students excluded from class, was reported missing (OC Media).
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no hostilities on Azerbaijani territory. The hijab protests are the most significant domestic unrest in years but have so far involved detentions rather than lethal violence. Over the next 90 days, expect the government to contain the protests with arrests, internet restrictions and pressure on activists. Religious mobilisation, Iranian media amplification and friction with Turkey (Aliyev's veiled criticism of Ankara, closer ties with Israel and a planned Netanyahu visit) add instability. With Armenia, the peace track is slow but intact, and both sides are treating the Shaki soldier case as criminal. A sustained escalation of the hijab protests into violent clashes, or a pattern of armed incidents with Armenia or Iran, would warrant a review toward HIGH.

regions.name: Sahel
overview: Sudan remains the region's most intense war and is escalating around El Obeid: by 14 October the RSF had massed forces from Darfur and West Kordofan on the city's approaches and was striking power plants and fuel stations, prompting Western and US warnings of an imminent assault, while a 9 October drone strike near a displacement site in Blue Nile's Wad al-Mahi killed at least 30–41 civilians; al-Burhan's 7 October rejection of talks closes off any near-term truce.

North-east Nigeria saw the sharpest jihadist escalation of the week: after the 6–7 October Kukawa assault, ISWAP overran the Mairari base in Guzamala LGA on 13 October, killing an estimated 10–15 soldiers plus CJTF members and civilians, despite a claimed 10 October airstrike that killed 40+ fighters in the same LGA; in the north-west, an 11 October bandit ambush on an army-escorted trader convoy in Zamfara left about 22 feared dead.

In the central Sahel the JNIM–IS Sahel war-within-a-war continues: IS claimed (via Amaq) to have killed about 400 JNIM fighters at Ganadaouri, Oudalan province (Burkina Faso), on 9 October — an unverified and almost certainly inflated figure — while Mali's junta consolidates in Kidal after the FLA's 6 October withdrawal and JNIM keeps up IED attacks on pro-government militias in Mopti and pressure on the fuel corridors.

Information conditions are poor: no independently verified attack in Niger and few in Mali and Burkina Faso were found for 9–16 October, which reflects junta information blackouts and lagging wire coverage rather than calm; all threat levels are unchanged (Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Sudan, Nigeria CRITICAL; Chad HIGH; Mauritania MODERATE), with Chad's 14 October letter of intent with France to restore defence cooperation the main diplomatic shift.

countries.name: Mali
incidents: 8 Oct — Baïma, Mopti region: JNIM claimed an IED strike on a vehicle of state-backed militias, part of its continuing campaign against pro-government auxiliaries in central Mali.

7–13 Oct — Kidal: FAMa said it consolidated its deployment in Kidal under Operation Dougoukoloko after the FLA's 'temporary' withdrawal; the town was reported largely emptied of residents, and no reporting confirmed government control of Tessalit or Tinzaouatène, which the FLA/JNIM held before the Kidal pullout.

Mid-Oct — Southern and western corridors: JNIM's fuel blockade remains in force, with Bamako still supplied by army-escorted tanker convoys; commentary on 15 Oct highlighted the strain on the Dakar–Bamako corridor. No new mass-casualty attack was independently confirmed for 9–16 Oct.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: JNIM and the FLA still hold territory and conduct regular attacks on state forces and militias, and the Kidal recapture does not change that. Over the next 90 days the junta and Africa Corps will likely try to extend from Kidal toward Aguelhok, Tessalit and Tinzaouatène, while the FLA shifts to ambushes, drones and IEDs against stretched supply lines in the Kidal region. JNIM remains the main threat: expect further garrison assaults in central and western Mali on the Dioura model, IED and drone attacks around Mopti/Sévaré, and continued interdiction of fuel convoys on the Sikasso, Kayes and Senegal corridors. Civilian reprisals in the north and displacement toward Mauritania and Algeria are likely; heavy losses keep the risk of internal military discontent elevated.

countries.name: Niger
incidents: 9–16 Oct — Nationwide: No independently verified, dated attack was located for this window; the junta's restrictions on reporting mean this should be read as an information gap, not a lull.

26 Sep (most recent major incident) — Birni-N'Konni area, Tahoua region: An ISSP attack killed more than 30 soldiers, following the c. 23 Sep ambush on a gendarme convoy near Abala-Filingué (Tillabéri); ISSP claimed both, with combined security-force losses above 50.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: ISSP mass-casualty attacks in late September and the August Niamey mutiny show sustained insurgency and acute regime instability, and a week without reporting does not indicate a reduced threat. Over the next 90 days further ISSP ambushes on army and gendarmerie convoys in Tillabéri and attacks along the Tahoua–Dosso belt toward the Nigeria border are likely, with JNIM pressure in the south-west toward Benin. The junta will keep prioritising regime protection with Africa Corps backing, purges and prosecutions of critics, which keeps morale low and a further coup or mutiny attempt a realistic possibility. Casualty figures will continue to surface late, via ISSP claims and anonymous sources.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
incidents: 9 Oct — Ganadaouri, Oudalan province: IS Sahel's Amaq agency claimed it repelled a large JNIM offensive in about 90 minutes of fighting and killed around 400 JNIM fighters; the figure is unverified and likely inflated, but confirms continued heavy JNIM–IS Sahel fighting in the north.
9–16 Oct — Nationwide: No independently verified attack on Burkinabè army or VDP positions was located in wire reporting for this window, consistent with the junta's ongoing information blackout.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: two jihadist groups fight the state and each other across much of the territory, and the absence of reported attacks reflects the blackout rather than calm. Over the next 90 days the JNIM–IS Sahel contest for Oudalan and Liptako-Gourma will likely continue to produce high-casualty clashes, while JNIM keeps seizing army and VDP posts in the North, East and Boucle du Mouhoun and maintains the sieges of Djibo, Sebba and Titao. Large garrison assaults on the Malian model remain likely as the dry season begins. Analysts should rely on group claims, displacement data and cross-border reporting, and watch for signs of instability within the junta in Ouagadougou.

countries.name: Sudan
incidents: 9 Oct — Wad al-Mahi, Blue Nile: A drone strike near a displacement site and informal gold-mining area killed at least 30 people according to local authorities (31 per the UN, 41 per Emergency Lawyers), mostly women and children; the Blue Nile government blamed the RSF and claimed the drone was launched from Ethiopia, which Ethiopia denies.

c. 10 Oct — Al-Nuhud and Gbeish, West Kordofan: A local monitor said SAF drone strikes killed at least 16 civilians over 48 hours, including 12 in a municipal building used as a shelter for displaced families; unverified.

14 Oct — El Obeid, North Kordofan: Western governments and the US warned the RSF against an imminent attack on the city after RSF drone strikes on power plants and fuel stations caused widespread blackouts and water cuts, as RSF forces from Darfur and West Kordofan massed around En Nahud, Al-Khuwei and the city's approaches.
7 Oct — Sudan (national): Army chief al-Burhan rejected negotiations and vowed to retake all territory from the RSF; clashes in Blue Nile displaced more than 5,500 people over three days.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: full-scale war continues on multiple fronts with near-daily deadly drone strikes and ground fighting. Over the next 90 days the decisive contest is likely around El Obeid: the RSF will probably attempt a siege or assault using El Fasher-style tactics — encirclement, strikes on power, water and fuel, and drone attacks on civilian sites — while SAF tries to exploit the al-Mazroub gain westward toward En Nahud and Al-Khuwei. Blue Nile is emerging as a second drone front with a cross-border dimension that risks drawing Ethiopia–Sudan tensions into the conflict. With al-Burhan rejecting talks, a humanitarian truce is unlikely; expect high civilian casualties, new displacement into Chad and South Sudan, and deepening famine.

countries.name: Chad
incidents: 14 Oct — N'Djamena/Paris: France and Chad signed a letter of intent to restore defence cooperation on a new basis, the first formal step since the French withdrawal.

4 Oct — Eastern border: UNHCR's September border-monitoring report said security remains the main driver of arrivals, after daily crossings at Tiné rose from about 20 to 200–400 in mid-September; more than 55,000 Sudanese have entered Chad in 2026 and the regional response is only 18% funded.

9–16 Oct — Eastern border and Lac province: No new cross-border strike or Boko Haram attack on Chadian territory was confirmed; the Lac province state of emergency and night curfew in force since May remain in place.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained: Chad faces recurring Boko Haram violence around Lake Chad (state of emergency since the May base attack) and a credible risk of spillover from Sudan, but no ongoing hostilities on its own territory this week. Over the next 90 days, a likely RSF push on El Obeid and continued Darfur fighting will sustain high refugee arrivals at Tiné and Adré, straining underfunded camps and raising inter-communal and weapons-proliferation risks. A repeat of the SAF/RSF cross-border strikes seen in March and August remains plausible and would justify a return to CRITICAL. The renewed defence relationship with France and ties with Haftar's LNA point to Déby diversifying security partners while watching rebel activity in the north.

countries.name: Mauritania
incidents: 9–16 Oct — Nationwide: No significant new security incident on Mauritanian territory was found in this window.

Sep–Oct (ongoing) — Hodh Chargui/Mali border: UNHCR registered about 290,000 Malian refugees in Hodh Chargui as of July, new arrivals continue to report threats and forced displacement by jihadists, and accusations persist that FAMa and Africa Corps killed or disappeared Mauritanian herders across the border.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained: Mauritania has no organised armed violence on its territory; its risk comes from border friction with Mali, refugee pressure and migration. Over the next 90 days, FAMa/Africa Corps operations in the north after the Kidal recapture and JNIM activity in western Mali are likely to drive further refugee arrivals into Mbera and risk new incidents involving Mauritanian herders, keeping Nouakchott–Bamako relations tense; Nouakchott will likely continue its containment approach of protests and precautionary measures. Migrant interdiction and expulsions on the Atlantic route will continue to draw human-rights criticism. A JNIM attack inside Mauritania or an armed border clash would justify a return to HIGH.

countries.name: Nigeria
incidents: 13 Oct — Mairari, Guzamala LGA, Borno: ISWAP/Boko Haram fighters overran a military base, killing an estimated 10–15 soldiers plus CJTF members and at least four to five civilians, burning military vehicles and parts of the village and wounding more than 20; the military has not issued an official toll.

10 Oct — Badu village, Guzamala LGA, Borno: The military said a precision airstrike on an ISWAP gathering preparing attacks on Sector 3 troops killed more than 40 fighters, including a senior commander; not independently verified.

11 Oct — Gurusu–Gwashi road, Bukkuyum LGA, Zamfara: Suspected bandits ambushed traders travelling under army escort to a weekly market; about 22 people, including security personnel, are feared dead, with no official statement yet.
12–14 Oct — Daffo, Bokkos LGA, Plateau: Gunmen shot the traditional ruler (Mishkaham Bokkos) at his residence on the night of 12 Oct; he died of his injuries on 14 Oct.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: two ISWAP base assaults in a week (Kukawa 6–7 Oct, Mairari 13 Oct) and deadly bandit ambushes on escorted convoys confirm sustained insurgency with regular military deaths. Over the next 90 days, ISWAP is likely to keep up multi-axis night raids on isolated bases in Guzamala, Kukawa and Marte as the dry season improves mobility, with the military answering through airstrikes of uncertain effect. In the north-west, bandit attacks and kidnappings in Zamfara, Katsina and Sokoto will continue, including on army-escorted convoys, while killings in Plateau's Bokkos area risk intercommunal reprisals. Security failures will feed political pressure ahead of the election cycle.

regions.name: Asia-Pacific
overview: Pakistan's security crisis now has a constitutional dimension: on 11 October Islamabad imposed emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, suspending the elected PTI government and citing militant violence. PTI protests turned violent on 13–14 October. On the Durand Line, Pakistani and Taliban forces clashed again in Kurram and Paktia on 10 October after the Moscow Format talks ended on 5 October without agreement.

North Korea fired at least two ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area on 12 October, one flying more than 900 km on an irregular, possibly hypersonic path. It was its fourth launch in about a month and came days after South Korea's first hypersonic missile test, overseen by President Lee. The unresolved DMZ mine dispute and this test-for-test dynamic keep the risk of escalation on the peninsula high.

Myanmar's Arakan Army is pressing toward the junta's last Rakhine strongholds: there is fighting at the entrance to Sittwe and on Nga Pyi Island, where the military has made amphibious and gunboat assaults since 7 October, and pressure on the Kyaukphyu naval base. The air force has kept up mass strikes elsewhere, including about 30 sorties on villages in Sagaing on 11–12 October.

Chinese military signalling is rising again after the post-summit lull: PLA 'joint combat readiness patrols' crossed the Taiwan Strait median line on 9 and 14 October, and the carrier Liaoning flew operations inside Japan's EEZ south of Ishigaki on 14 October, ahead of the US-Japan exercise Keen Sword (19–29 October). Chinese maritime militia swarms also continued in the Philippines' Kalayaan waters.

countries.name: North Korea
incidents: 12 Oct — Pyongyang area: North Korea fired at least two ballistic missiles toward the East Sea about 17 minutes apart, starting at about 09:20. Japan said one flew about 220 km and the other more than 910 km on an 'irregular' trajectory, possibly hypersonic; South Korea's JCS called it a show of force.

12 Oct — Pyongyang: This was the regime's fourth launch in about a month and came days after South Korea's first hypersonic missile test (8 Oct). Reports differ on the number of missiles, and KCNA described the launch as a 'tactical ballistic missile'.

13 Oct — Honolulu/Seoul: US Indo-Pacific Command said the launch posed no immediate threat and reaffirmed its defence commitment to its allies. Seoul's presidential office called the launches violations of UN Security Council resolutions.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect Pyongyang to keep matching South Korean and allied capability demonstrations with launches of its own. The 3 and 12 October tests suggest an effort to field hypersonic and manoeuvring systems, both intermediate-range and tactical, that can evade allied missile defences. North Korea still refuses to accept responsibility for the DMZ mines, and border fortification continues, so the border remains the most likely place for a kinetic incident. Further launches are likely around Keen Sword (19–29 October) and other allied drills. A nuclear test remains a low-probability, high-impact wildcard.

countries.name: Myanmar
incidents: 7–13 Oct — Nga Pyi Island, Sittwe, Rakhine State: Since 7 Oct the military has sent six gunboats and about a dozen speedboats, backed by airstrikes and artillery, to retake the Kaladan delta island. Local sources say scores of soldiers were killed or captured in the first three days, and the AA has seized regime sentry posts at the entrance to Sittwe (Irrawaddy, 13 Oct).

11–12 Oct — Sagaing Region: Waves of junta airstrikes killed at least five civilians and injured 23, including about 30 strikes on four villages in Wetlet Township. Three bombing runs hit a monastery compound sheltering displaced people in Seikkhun village, Shwebo Township, killing two people and wounding eight (DVB).

8–12 Oct — Mindon Township, Magway Region: At least three civilians were killed and three injured during fighting between the Arakan Army and regime forces, as a military counteroffensive pushes from Magway toward Rakhine (DVB, 14 Oct).

7–8 Oct — Kyaukphyu and Bhamo: Reports say the junta is evacuating dependents and supplies from the Taung Maw Oo naval base after the AA captured outposts guarding it on 4 Oct. In Kachin, KIA forces overran junta positions near Bhamo University and jets then bombed nearby villages.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, the Arakan Army is likely to tighten its grip on Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, the junta's last Rakhine strongholds and the site of Chinese strategic investments. The military will respond with amphibious counter-attacks, a ground push from Magway and intensive air strikes. Expect continued mass-casualty strikes on towns, monasteries and displacement camps in Rakhine, Sagaing, Karenni and Kachin. The possible fall of the Kyaukphyu naval base would be a major turning point and could draw greater Chinese diplomatic involvement. No negotiated de-escalation is in sight.

countries.name: Pakistan
incidents: 10 Oct — Kurram district, KP / Paktia, Afghanistan: The ISPR said troops broke up a TTP infiltration attempt supported by fire from Afghan Taliban posts, killing 12 TTP and Taliban fighters, and that one Pakistani soldier was killed. The Taliban accused Pakistan of firing first, and there were further exchanges of fire in Dand Patan and Aryob Zazi; Pakistan closed the border.

11 Oct — Peshawar: The federal government imposed a state of emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under Articles 232 and 234, citing rising militant violence. It suspended the PTI provincial government, and Chief Minister Sohail Afridi was reportedly detained as the PTI march on Islamabad collapsed amid arrests.

13–14 Oct — Bara (Khyber district) and Peshawar: PTI protests turned violent. Protesters reportedly torched a NADRA office and briefly held police hostage in Bara, and PTI claimed one person was killed and more than a dozen injured when police opened fire; a Peshawar hospital received more than a dozen injured, including four policemen.

10–13 Oct — Balochistan: CTD police killed 10 suspected 'Fitna al-Hindustan' (Baloch) militants in Barkhan on 10 Oct, and the ISPR said five more were killed in Washuk on the night of 12–13 Oct. CRSS reported 829 violence-linked deaths in Balochistan in Q3 2026, up from 265 in Q2.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, Pakistan faces a two-front security crisis compounded by political turmoil. The Taliban conflict will continue as border clashes and possible new air strikes into Afghanistan, with no diplomatic track after the failed Moscow talks. TTP/IMP violence in KP and BLA/BLF operations in Balochistan will continue at record levels. Governor's rule in KP is likely to deepen unrest among PTI supporters, divert security forces and weaken local legitimacy for counter-terrorism. Mass-casualty attacks on police and military targets, and further protest violence, are likely. Court challenges to the emergency could prolong the crisis.

countries.name: India
incidents: 10–12 Oct — Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul districts, Manipur: Fresh Kuki-Naga clashes killed nine to ten people, with four each in Kamjong and Kangpokpi, including Naga villagers or village guards at Makui Asang. Houses were torched, residents fled, and a 24-hour highway shutdown and restrictions were imposed.

12 Oct — Poonch, Jammu and Kashmir (LoC): Four Pakistani infiltrators, including a Lashkar-e-Taiba commander named as Mohammad Faizan, were killed when they set off an anti-infiltration minefield along the Line of Control; officials said it was the first incident of this kind on the LoC in 2026.

Ongoing — Manipur: With the latest killings, Naga-Kuki-Zo violence has killed well over 36 people in 2026. The state government has called a high-level meeting with community leaders while the Chief Minister holds talks in New Delhi.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, the Kuki-Naga conflict in Manipur's hill districts is likely to see further lethal raids, arson and highway blockades, with the October killings raising the risk of reprisal cycles that central forces struggle to contain. In Jammu and Kashmir, infiltration attempts across the LoC in Poonch and Rajouri and encounters in the Jammu-region forests will continue until winter closes the passes. India-Pakistan tension remains a background factor, but no direct military incident was reported.

countries.name: China
incidents: 13–14 Oct — East China Sea / south of Ishigaki: The carrier Liaoning and three destroyers transited past Okinawa and Miyako into the Pacific and conducted flight operations about 155 miles south of Ishigaki, inside Japan's EEZ. Beijing called it 'annual routine training' not aimed at any country.

9 and 14 Oct — Taiwan Strait: The PLA flew 'joint combat readiness patrols', with nine aircraft crossing the median line on each date and coordinating with naval vessels, a rise from the near-zero air activity around the Xi-Trump summit.

9 Oct — Kota Island, Spratlys: The Philippine Coast Guard drove away the Chinese maritime militia vessel CMMV 9622 and 22 fishing boats, the same mothership it repelled on 28 Sep; Manila called it a 'coordinated militia operation'.
6 Oct — Beijing: The Foreign Ministry restated its sovereignty claims over Scarborough Shoal and the Spratlys in response to Philippine harassment complaints, and opposed US arms sales to Taiwan.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect Beijing to step back up from the post-summit lull: more median-line patrols, carrier operations in the western Pacific during and after Keen Sword, and continued coast-guard and militia pressure on the Philippines, Japan's Senkakus and Vietnam's claims. A large named drill around Taiwan remains possible if Washington moves on the paused arms package. China's own territory faces no armed threat and internal security is stable; the main risk is a confrontation caused by its own forces at sea or in the air.

countries.name: Taiwan
incidents: 9 Oct — Taiwan Strait: The MND reported a PLA 'joint combat readiness patrol' in which nine aircraft crossed the median line in coordination with naval vessels.
11–12 Oct — Around Taiwan: The MND logged 12 PLA aircraft sorties, six PLAN vessels and three official ships on 11 Oct, and four sorties on 12 Oct, one of which entered the southern ADIZ.

14 Oct — Around Taiwan: The MND detected nine PLA aircraft sorties, all crossing the median line, along with six PLAN ships and six official ships, and responded with combat air patrols, navy ships and coastal missile systems.
Sep (reported Oct) — Taiwan's waters: The coast guard detected 244 Chinese vessels around Taiwan in September, about 60% of them China Coast Guard ships, up from 55 in June and 30 in May.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect the return of median-line air patrols, a constant navy and coast-guard presence, and grey-zone pressure at Kinmen and Pratas. The sharp rise in Chinese coast guard vessel counts points to a strategy of normalising 'law enforcement' around the island. A large-scale drill becomes likely if the US unfreezes the $14 billion arms package or Taipei takes steps Beijing considers provocative. Taipei will press ahead with higher defence spending and asymmetric programmes.

countries.name: Philippines
incidents: 9–10 Oct — Kota Island (Loaita Cay), Kalayaan/Spratlys: The PCG repelled the Chinese maritime militia vessel CMMV 9622 and 22 sampans from territorial waters, reporting illegal fishing and waste dumping; spokesman Tarriela called it a 'coordinated militia operation'.

15 Oct — Lawak (Nanshan) Island, Spratlys: The PCG chased away a Chinese fishing vessel and four smaller boats launched from a mother ship, citing violations of the Fisheries Code and the Maritime Zones Act.

9 Oct (reported) — South China Sea and Luzon Strait: USNI News counted at least six dangerous Philippine-Chinese encounters since 1 Oct, at Scarborough, Second Thomas Shoal and in the Spratlys. These included a new front off Batanes, where China Coast Guard cutters escorted the survey vessel J High K7.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect continued CCG blocking, ramming and water-cannon incidents, PLA air intercepts over Scarborough and militia swarming in the Kalayaan islands, as well as a new contest in the Luzon Strait and Batanes. Manila's participation in Keen Sword with Japan and the US will draw Chinese criticism and possibly sharper signalling at sea. A serious-injury or fatal incident, or a mid-air collision, would raise the risk of Mutual Defense Treaty consultations and justify an upgrade. Mindanao and NPA violence on land remains low-level.

countries.name: South Korea
incidents: 8 Oct — South Korea: President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country's first test of a domestically developed hypersonic missile, which separated, manoeuvred and hit a test target; it was a rare presidential showcase of a missile test.

12 Oct — Seoul: The JCS detected North Korean ballistic missile launches from the Pyongyang area, one flying more than 900 km, and called them a show of force in response to Seoul's hypersonic test. The presidential office called them UN resolution violations and urged an immediate halt.

12 Oct — Seoul: Seoul maintained its demand for a North Korean apology over the DMZ mine blast that wounded three soldiers and is considering steps to force one; Pyongyang rejects the joint ROK-UNC finding that North Korea planted the mines.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, the peninsula is in a test-for-test cycle: Seoul's hypersonic programme and allied drills will be met with North Korean launches. Combined with the unresolved DMZ mine dispute and Seoul's hint at measures to compel an apology, this raises the risk of a border incident. President Lee's engagement policy is under domestic pressure. Watch for any resumption of loudspeakers or leaflets, further mine or drone incidents, and North Korean reactions to Keen Sword.

countries.name: Vietnam
incidents: 12 Oct — Beijing/Hanoi: National Assembly Chairman Tran Thanh Man began an official visit to China and met Chinese friendship delegations, signalling that Hanoi is keeping political channels open alongside its maritime protests.

12–15 Oct — Hanoi: Defence Minister Phan Van Giang held talks with Lao counterpart Gen. Khamliang Outhakaysone, against a background of commentary on China's growing military footprint in Cambodia (Ream) and Laos.

28 Aug (continuing) — Paracels: Vietnam's formal protest against Chinese construction, assessed as radar facilities, on Yagong Island and at Antelope Reef still stands; no new Vietnam-China maritime incident was reported this week.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, Vietnam is likely to continue its two-track policy: high-level political engagement with Beijing, as with the Tran Thanh Man visit, alongside formal protests over the Paracels build-up and accelerated fortification of its own Spratly features (runway, harbours). Watch for Chinese pressure on Vietnamese fishermen in the Paracels and for reactions to Vietnam's Spratly runway. A direct naval confrontation remains unlikely.

countries.name: Japan
incidents: 13–14 Oct — Southwest islands: The Chinese carrier Liaoning and three destroyers were tracked southwest of the Danjo Islands. On 14 Oct the carrier launched and recovered aircraft about 155 miles south of Ishigaki, inside Japan's EEZ, before sailing past Okinawa and Miyako into the Pacific. The JASDF scrambled fighters and the MSDF deployed JS Yugiri, a P-1 and a P-3C.

12 Oct — Tokyo: The Defence Ministry reported two North Korean ballistic missiles about 17 minutes apart, flying about 220 km and more than 910 km on an irregular trajectory; both landed outside Japan's EEZ.

Upcoming 19–29 Oct — Japan: The US-Japan exercise Keen Sword is set to involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 260 aircraft and 40 vessels, with Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the Philippines taking part.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained; watch for upgrade. Over the next 90 days, expect Chinese and possibly Russian responses to Keen Sword and to the Typhon deployment, including carrier operations near the Nansei islands, joint bomber patrols and strait transits, while China Coast Guard pressure around the Senkakus stays high. North Korea's longer-range tests raise the risk of overflights or impacts inside the EEZ. A close-quarters air or maritime incident, or a missile landing in the EEZ, would justify an upgrade to HIGH.

countries.name: Indonesia
incidents: 9 Oct — Sungai Frambu, Maybrat Regency, Southwest Papua: The TNI said its troops shot dead three members of the Free Papua Movement (OPM/TPNPB) in a gunfight. This came amid intensified operations over the previous two weeks following attacks on civilians attributed to insurgents.

8 Oct — Seradala District, Yahukimo Regency, Highland Papua: Human rights monitors report that a Papuan civilian was killed after being detained by Marines personnel, which they allege was an unlawful execution in custody.

Late Sep (reported Oct) — Intan Jaya, Central Papua: The TNI said four TPNPB-OPM rebels were killed in a clash, part of an escalating cycle after the September killings of civil servants and a driver in Jayawijaya.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect a continued cycle of TPNPB attacks on non-Papuan civilians, infrastructure workers and isolated posts, and intensified TNI and Cartenz operations with lethal clashes, allegations of extrajudicial killings and new displacement in the Highlands, Central and Southwest Papua. Jakarta shows no sign of moving toward dialogue, so deadly violence is likely to continue weekly or fortnightly.

countries.name: Thailand
incidents: 15 Oct — The Hague: Thailand and Cambodia held a second round of closed UNCLOS conciliation talks on their maritime boundary in the Gulf of Thailand, scheduled to run until 18 Oct.

1 Oct (published) — Phnom Penh/UN: In a letter to the UN, Cambodia rejected Thai border claims, demanded an end to what it called the 'unlawful military occupation' of border areas and urged a return to the Joint Boundary Commission and full implementation of the December 2025 ceasefire.

1 Oct — Tak Bai, Narathiwat: A bomb hidden in a motorcycle sidecar exploded outside a PT petrol station, with no initial reports of casualties; it was the most recent reported insurgent bombing in the Deep South.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, the Thai-Cambodian land ceasefire is likely to hold. The rhetoric at the UN and local trench and landmine disputes keep a small risk of shooting incidents, while the maritime dispute moves slowly through conciliation. In the Deep South, expect intermittent bombings, arson and targeted shootings of rangers by BRN-linked cells, with periodic coordinated waves but no peace breakthrough.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 12 Oct — Dhaka: The Human Rights Support Society reported 183 incidents of political violence in July–September, with 17 dead and 1,227 injured. Intra-BNP factional clashes were the largest share; BNP-Jamaat clashes killed two and BNP-Awami League clashes killed two.

15 Oct — Gazipur: An Awami League leader died after falling ill in custody at Gazipur District Jail, according to local media; the party demanded an independent probe into rising custodial deaths of its members.
8 Oct — Nationwide: Ahead of Durga Puja, the banned Awami League raised alarms about violence against Hindus; no major communal incident was confirmed in reporting found this week.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect continued low-level but deadly political violence, driven mainly by BNP factional rivalry and BNP-Jamaat competition, together with sporadic Awami League flash protests and crude-bomb attacks in Dhaka met by mass arrests. Custodial deaths and the new security laws, including the RAB rebrand, raise the risk of abusive policing. An upgrade would be warranted if ICT death sentences are carried out or if unrest becomes widely lethal.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 9 Oct — Nagoda, Kalutara: A restaurant owner was shot dead and his wife injured outside their restaurant in the latest underworld-linked shooting; police later arrested three suspects for aiding and abetting.

14 Oct — Southern Province: The Police Special Task Force arrested the main gunman of the 'Palani Canister' gang and a motorcycle rider, who were allegedly preparing to kill the child of a man shot dead earlier.
3 Oct — Kosgoda: A suspect fired at police during a raid on a house where an underworld retaliation killing was allegedly being planned; one suspect was injured and another arrested.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Over the next 90 days, Sri Lanka's security situation will stay dominated by gang and narcotics-related gun violence in the Western and Southern provinces, met by police and STF operations under the anti-drug drive. No indicators of insurgent, terrorist or communal conflict were observed.

regions.name: Americas
overview: Colombia remains the region's only active armed conflict and its drone war is intensifying: within one week a soldier was killed by a drone-dropped explosive in La Vega (Cauca), a policeman was shot dead by FARC dissidents near Tulua, and on 14 October an ELN drone swarm wounded nine soldiers at a base in San Jose del Palmar (Choco). Infobae counts a record 176 drone attacks on security forces in 2026 so far, 90 of them attributed to the ELN.

Haiti's political transition has stalled: on 6 October the Provisional Electoral Council postponed the 13 December elections indefinitely, citing gang violence, blocked roads and only 769,000 registered voters. The UN Security Council renewed the gang sanctions regime for 13 months on 15 October, while the Gang Suppression Force, at about 1,500 of a planned 5,500 personnel, struggles to protect communities such as Gros-Morne, whose mayor is urging residents to flee gang-held areas.

Criminal violence along the Andean–Pacific belt continues at a steady pace rather than escalating. In Ecuador, gunmen killed a 16-year-old student and two men in Machala on 14 October, and on 15 October Operation Muralla arrested four Comandos de la Frontera leaders. In Peru, extortion gangs killed another colectivo driver in San Juan de Lurigancho on 13 October, but transport unions ruled out a strike on 9 October and are coordinating with police instead.

Political pressure in Venezuela and Bolivia is being channelled into mobilisation, not violence. Machado says Washington has excluded her from a third round of government–opposition talks in Caracas, and her platform has called a nationwide march for 22 October to demand an election date. In Bolivia, Morales-aligned groups postponed their 13 October march against the diesel price rise after police and the army deployed to nine access points around La Paz. In Cuba, a generation deficit of more than 1,600 MW is fuelling repeated neighbourhood protests, including two in Cabanas (Artemisa) within four days.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 14 Oct — Caracas: Henrique Capriles accused acting President Delcy Rodriguez of trying to extend her interim mandate to 2030, arguing that the Constitution requires elections when the head of state is absent.

15 Oct — Nationwide: The Comando Con Venezuela, the platform of Maria Corina Machado and Edmundo Gonzalez, called a nationwide march for 22 October to demand a presidential election date, proposing 24 July 2027.

15–16 Oct — Caracas/Washington: Machado said the US had excluded her from the third round of talks since August, held in Caracas this week between the Rodriguez government and part of the opposition. The State Department replied that her party had been invited and that she is free to return home.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No new armed clashes were reported this week. The situation is one of political tension and managed repression without significant casualties, and US–Venezuela cooperation keeps the risk of external military action low. Over the next 90 days, the main domestic flashpoint is the electoral timetable: the 22 October nationwide march and any attempt by Machado to return will test whether security forces and colectivos tolerate mass opposition rallies. Expect further incremental prisoner releases alongside short-term detentions, and growing friction between the Machado camp and a US-sponsored dialogue that excludes it. The border states (Tachira, Apure, Zulia) remain the main security risk as Colombia's offensive pushes the ELN and FARC dissidents east, following the 28 September National Guard–ELN clash in Junin (Tachira). Upgrade to HIGH if opposition rallies are violently dispersed with casualties, if border clashes become recurring and deadly, or if US–Venezuela cooperation breaks down.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 10 Oct — La Vega, Cauca: A soldier was killed when an explosive was dropped from a drone onto army troops. Infobae lists the attack among those attributed to the ELN.

10–13 Oct — Catatumbo, Norte de Santander: A military bombing against FARC dissidents killed four alleged members, including a 16-year-old girl according to Medicina Legal. Three soldiers were wounded by a minefield during the same operation.

11–13 Oct — Tulua (Valle del Cauca) and Silvia (Cauca): Gunmen of the FARC dissident 57th Front killed police officer Diego Andres Sanabria Romero and wounded another in rural Tulua, and police shot dead one attacker. On 13 October, dissidents attacked police in the urban centre of Silvia.

14 Oct — San Jose del Palmar, Choco: A drone swarm detonated 21 grenades on the base of Military Engineers Battalion No. 15, wounding nine soldiers, who were evacuated to Medellin. The army blamed the ELN's Ernesto Che Guevara Front.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. This week brought fatal drone and small-arms attacks on the army and police in Cauca and Valle del Cauca, a first reported drone-swarm attack on a military base in Choco, and lethal air strikes by the state in Catatumbo. These match the definition of a sustained insurgency with regular deaths and territory held by armed groups. Over the next 90 days, expect weekly drone and explosive attacks on police substations and bases in Cauca, Huila, Valle del Cauca, Choco and Norte de Santander. The ELN is increasingly using massed drones, and fibre-optic drones are reducing the value of jammers. Massacres are on track to exceed 110 for the year. The De la Espriella government's bombing campaign will raise the risk of civilian and minor casualties and the political controversy that follows, and will push armed units across the Venezuelan border. Watch for the rollout of the national anti-drone shield, the first mass-casualty drone attack in an urban area, and retaliation against cities such as Popayan and Cali.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 6–7 Oct — Port-au-Prince: The Provisional Electoral Council postponed the 13 December general elections and the 21 February 2027 run-off indefinitely, citing gang violence, roads closed by gang threats, and only 769,000 registered voters. Several gang-controlled municipalities have no registration centres.

Week to 14 Oct — Gros-Morne, Artibonite: Mayor Hubert Ceneac urged residents to evacuate communal sections held by the Kokorat San Ras gang. The death toll from the late-September GSF operation and gang reprisals has risen to at least 34, including 19 civilians. Police said they had not been informed of the evacuation plan.
14 Oct — Port-au-Prince area: CNN reported coming under fire while accompanying Haitian police trying to retake hilltop villages from gangs.

15 Oct — New York: The UN Security Council renewed the Haiti sanctions regime for 13 months, including the arms embargo, travel ban and asset freeze. About 1.5 million people, 12% of the population, are now displaced.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Gangs still control most of Port-au-Prince and large parts of Artibonite and the Centre. Insecurity has now forced the indefinite postponement of national elections, which confirms that the state has lost control over a significant part of its territory. Over the next 90 days, the political transition will lack a timetable, increasing the risk of disputes over who governs and of gang leaders using the vacuum to gain leverage. The GSF, at under 30% of planned strength, can carry out local clearance operations, such as from its new base in Grepin near Gros-Morne, but cannot hold ground. Each advance is likely to trigger reprisal massacres against civilians, as in Gros-Morne. Expect continued kidnappings of officials and professionals, more displacement along National Road 5 and in the Centre department, and further raids in Cite Soleil, Tabarre and Kenscoff. Watch for a new electoral calendar, the pace of further troop arrivals, and enforcement of the renewed arms embargo.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 9 Oct — Nationwide: Available generation was 1,250 MW against an estimated demand of 2,900 MW, about 43% of requirements. In Artemisa province, outages remain at 18 hours or more a day.
9 Oct — Cabanas (Mariel), Artemisa: Residents protested in the street at night against prolonged power cuts.

14 Oct — Cabanas (Mariel), Artemisa: Residents held a second street protest within four days over blackouts. There were no confirmed reports of arrests or clashes, and the account rests on a witness quoted by CiberCuba.
14 Oct (reported) — Nationwide: The NGO Cubalex said that in September, incommunicado detention in Cuban prisons reached its highest level of the year after protests inside detention centres.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. There is no armed conflict, but generation now covers well under half of demand, and the resulting collapse of basic services is producing recurring neighbourhood protests and tighter repression, including in prisons. This meets the HIGH definition. Over the next 90 days, another nationwide grid collapse is likely given fuel scarcity and the late hurricane season, and each one tends to trigger a wave of pot-banging, street blockades and targeted arrests. The security apparatus remains cohesive, and its standard tactic of temporarily restoring power to protesting neighbourhoods has so far kept unrest local. Upgrade to CRITICAL only if protests coordinate across several cities, security forces use lethal force, or state control visibly erodes. Watch also for migration pressure and any change in US fuel restrictions.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 12–13 Oct — Santa Elena: Contract-killing attacks continued over the holiday period, including a shooting in the Coresa 1 neighbourhood outside Salinas. La Republica counted at least four people shot by hitmen from early 12 October.

14 Oct — Machala, El Oro: A 16-year-old student was shot dead on a city bus returning from school. In a separate shooting in the city centre, two men were killed and a 15-year-old girl was wounded. The Interior Ministry says 49 adolescents have died violently in El Oro this year.

15 Oct — Orellana, Sucumbios, Guayas: In Operation Muralla, 14 simultaneous raids arrested four alleged leaders of Comandos de la Frontera. The government links the group to the killing of 11 soldiers in Alto Punino, three police officers in La Joya de los Sachas, and 25 further deaths.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Gangs that the state treats as parties to an internal armed conflict continue to contest ports, prisons and border corridors. Homicides of minors are at a record 430 this year, and although total homicides fell 6.4% year on year to August, killings still exceed 20 a day. This meets the CRITICAL definition. With the curfew lifted, killings in Machala, Guayaquil, Duran and Santa Elena continue at night.
